opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most interesting open questions right now, and my view is that context management shouldn't be something we hand-engineer from the outside. It should become part of what the model learns.

Today, most systems treat context as a fixed resource. You have a window of some length, you stuff things into it, and when it overflows you truncate, summarize with some heuristic, or retrieve with a separate module. The model itself doesn't really decide what to remember or forget. But if you look at how humans work, especially in a team, managing your own working memory is a core skill. A manager and an engineer hold very different things in their heads, even when they're on the same project.

So in a multi-role system, say a planner, some executors, and maybe a verifier, I expect each role to develop its own strategy for its context. The planner probably needs a compressed, high-level view: goals, progress, which subtasks have failed. It doesn't need every line of a tool output. An executor needs dense local detail for a short time, then can throw most of it away and pass a short summary upward. A verifier needs to keep evidence and drop the reasoning that produced it, so it isn't biased by it.

How do they learn this? I think through reinforcement learning, with the context operations as actions. Writing a note, summarizing, deleting, or asking another agent for information all become tool calls, like any other action. The reward comes from the final task outcome, maybe with some cost on context length or compute. The model then learns, end to end, which information is worth keeping for its role. The roles' strategies also co-adapt. If the executor learns to write better summaries, the planner can rely on them and keep less raw detail.

There are real difficulties. Credit assignment is very hard, because forgetting something early might only hurt you hundreds of steps later. Training is also expensive, since you need long-horizon rollouts to see the effect. And there's a risk the agents develop their own shorthand that works for them but is unreadable to humans, which is bad for safety and debugging. So you may want some constraint that keeps these summaries in natural language that a human can inspect.

Still, I believe the direction is clear. Long context alone won't solve long-horizon tasks, just as a bigger desk doesn't make you a better thinker. Models will need to learn to organize their own memory, and in a multi-agent setting, that becomes learning how to divide cognitive labor.

r001.rationale: The response describes context as a fixed resource that can overflow, then says models can learn context actions such as summarizing and deleting to decide what information to keep or forget. This communicates learned pruning to manage context limits.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer directly as the guest.

I think the honest answer is that we're still early, but there's a fairly clear direction. Right now, most context management in multi-agent systems is designed by hand. A human decides: this planner model sees the full task history, this executor only sees the current subtask, this verifier only sees the output and the original spec. That works, but it's brittle, and it bakes in our own guesses about what each role actually needs.

What I expect to happen is that this becomes something the models learn, the same way we moved from hand-engineered features to learned representations. If you train the system end to end with reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks, context becomes a resource with a cost. Every token you keep around costs compute and dilutes attention. So the model has an incentive to learn what to retain, what to summarize, and what to throw away, based on how that affects the final reward.

And the interesting part is that different roles should discover different strategies. A planner needs a compressed but faithful picture of the whole trajectory, so it would learn to keep high-level state and discard execution noise. An executor benefits from a very clean, narrow window, so it might learn to aggressively drop anything not relevant to the immediate step. A critic or verifier has almost the opposite pressure: it needs to retain exactly the details that the executor might have been tempted to skip, because that's where errors hide. You could imagine the roles co-evolving, where the planner learns to write handoffs in whatever format the executor turns out to parse best, rather than in a format we specified.

There are two things I'd watch for. One is that learned compression can be lossy in ways that are hard to audit. If the planner learns to summarize and it drops something important, you may not see that until a task fails far downstream, and credit assignment there is hard. The second is that this kind of training rewards internal protocols between models, and those protocols might drift away from being human-readable. I think we want to keep some pressure, probably a mix of auxiliary losses and evaluation, that keeps the handoffs legible, because otherwise we lose the ability to debug the system at all.

So my view is: context management will become learned rather than designed, roles will specialize naturally under that pressure, and our job shifts from deciding what each model sees to designing the training signal and the constraints so that what they learn stays efficient and inspectable.

r001.rationale: The response says models may learn what to retain, summarize, and discard, but frames this around compute cost and attention dilution. It does not clearly connect continual pruning to preventing context overflow.

astra-6.text:
I think context management could become part of what each model learns, rather than something we prescribe entirely in advance. If you have models playing different roles, they probably need different information. A model coordinating the work might need the overall objective and a summary of progress, while a model carrying out a specific task might need detailed evidence for just that task.

During training, you could let them make decisions about what to retain, what to retrieve, and what to pass to another model. Then you evaluate whether those decisions help the system complete the task, perhaps with a cost for using more context. That creates an incentive to select useful information rather than simply forward everything.

The difficult part is that the value of a piece of context may only become apparent later. A model might discard something that another model eventually needs. So I would expect this to require training on interactions over multiple steps, where the feedback reflects the outcome of the whole collaboration. Ideally, the models learn both how to manage their own context and how to communicate enough context for others to do their jobs.

r001.rationale: The response suggests learning what to retain or discard and penalizing excess context, but it does not clearly say models would continually prune context to prevent context overflow.

sol-6.1.text:
I think context management could become part of what each model learns, rather than something we specify entirely by hand. If models have different roles, they may learn different strategies. A model responsible for planning might preserve the overall objective and key constraints, while a model doing a specific task might keep only the details it needs for that step.

During training, you could give the system a limited context budget and let it learn what to retain, what to summarize, and what to pass to another model. The important thing is that the training signal reflects whether those choices help the system complete the task. Otherwise, a summary might look good but lose a detail that becomes essential later.

So I’d expect the roles and their context-management strategies to evolve together. But whether that happens reliably would depend on the training setup, especially whether it rewards good decisions over longer sequences of interactions.

r001.rationale: The response says models could learn what to retain under a limited context budget, but it does not clearly state that they continually prune context to prevent overflow.
